slides.title: SlAIdy
slides.body:
Slides where the deck stays **markdown and SVG** — legible to you, to `git`,
and to the model you edit it with.

#### What this one slide is made of

| | |
|---|---|
| an animated figure | SVG, `@keyframes`, 6 kB |
| a formula | $r_{ui} = \mathbf{p}_u^\top \mathbf{q}_i$ |
| a table | this one |
| code | below |
| a link | [kordikp.github.io/slaidy](https://kordikp.github.io/slaidy/) |

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kordikp/slaidy && ./studio.sh
```

***

> Everything on this slide is text. The animation is 6 kB of SVG.
slides.notes: The figure is a twelve-second loop in four beats — you ask, it works, you correct it, it is pleased with you. All CSS keyframes, and it reads with the animation off, which is the rule every figure in this deck follows; a print takes one frame, so a loop that hides something would lose it.
slides.summary: Open on what the project is, and let the slide itself be the argument — everything the format can carry, on one slide.

slides.title: One material, two readers
slides.body:
A deck here is text: markdown for the words, SVG for the drawings.

That is not a storage decision. It is what lets **two very different readers work on
the same thing** — you, when you come back to a talk a year later; the model, when you
ask it to make a figure sparser or to cut what repeats.

> Neither has to take the other's word for what is on the slide.
slides.notes: The claim to resist making here is "first". Plenty of tools put a model beside a document. What is unusual is that both sides read the same artefact, at the same level of detail.
slides.summary: The idea the whole project turns on — the material has to be legible to everyone working on it.

slides.title: Who decides what
slides.notes: Every AI action in this editor produces a proposal you accept or discard, and one Ctrl-Z puts the slide back. The panel that reads a slide and says what it would change writes those changes into a box you can edit — striking a line out is how you disagree.
slides.summary: Draw the line: the argument, the cuts and the words are the author's; the drafts, the drawings and the criticism are the model's.

slides.title: A picture you can take apart
slides.body:
A bitmap can be shown and scaled. That is all: nobody can edit it, git cannot diff it,
and asking a model to change it means asking it to draw a new one and hope.

An SVG has parts with names. Move one, recolour one, ask for one fewer.

> 237 slides and 180 figures come to **1 MB**. The same deck as `.pptx` is 34.
slides.summary: Why figures are SVG and never bitmaps, and why that is also why the format is small.

slides.title: A deck is a folder of markdown
slides.body:
Slides are `.md`, figures are `.svg`, and the bundle the app opens is one `.json` that
carries both. Export gives back the same files you started with.

> Nothing the app can write is something only the app can read.
slides.summary: The file format, and what it means for a deck to outlive its editor.

slides.title: One stage, three surfaces
slides.notes: This is the invariant everything else leans on. A layout that only looks right in the editor is a bug, and the test suite measures both surfaces and requires them to agree.
slides.summary: Editor, projector and PDF draw the same 1280×720 stage from the same code.

slides.title: Editing where you read
slides.body:
Click a title to change it. Hover a paragraph for a grip to drag it, a `＋` to insert
below it, arrows to move it a step.

Click a figure and its editor opens on the drawing — select a shape, move it, recolour
it, join two boxes with an arrow that re-routes itself when either moves.
slides.summary: You edit on the slide itself, at the size the room will see.

slides.title: Ask, and argue back
slides.body:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Say what a slide is for** | one line, and it writes the slide to serve it |
| **Ask for changes** | *cut the third bullet, the figure already says it* |
| **Analyse this slide** | it writes what it would change into a box you can edit |
| **Suggest what goes here** | three named moves, with the question each answers |

***

> Strike out what you disagree with. What is left is what runs.
slides.summary: How the AI is actually used in practice — as a first draft and a critic, never as an author.

slides.title: Getting it out again
slides.body:
PDF through the browser's own print engine — nothing is uploaded. Markdown in the shape
you started with. One `.json` bundle carrying slides and figures. Or the whole deck as
an **article**, figures rasterised, ready to paste into Substack or a `.docx`.

<!-- gap -->

> Try it: <https://kordikp.github.io/slaidy/> · source: <https://github.com/kordikp/slaidy>
slides.notes: The editor is MIT, one file, no dependencies and no build step. The AI runs on capacity from CESNET e-INFRA CZ.
slides.summary: Close on the exits, because a format you cannot leave is a trap.

figs.fig-slaidy-hero:
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 450" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif">
  <style>
    /* Twelve seconds, four beats: you ask, it works, you correct it, it is
       pleased with you. Everything is drawn in its finished state, so with the
       animation off — printing, or a reader who asked for less motion — the
       picture still reads. */
    @keyframes ask    { 0%{opacity:0;transform:translateY(6px) scale(.9)} 6%,26%{opacity:1;transform:none}
                        34%,100%{opacity:0;transform:translateY(6px) scale(.9)} }
    @keyframes hover  { 0%,100%{transform:translateY(0)} 50%{transform:translateY(-5px)} }

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 450" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif">
  <style>
    @keyframes sweep { 0%{stroke-dashoffset:300} 60%,100%{stroke-dashoffset:0} }

  <rect width="800" height="450" rx="14" fill="#FAFAF7" stroke="#E5E7EB"/>

  <text x="221" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#065F46">yours</text>

  <text class="keep" x="88" y="192" font-size="13" fill="#065F46">which slide earns its place</text>
  <text class="keep" x="88" y="232" font-size="13" fill="#065F46">the arrangement, the words</text>
  <text class="keep" x="88" y="272" font-size="13" fill="#065F46">what is true</text>

  <rect x="414" y="72" width="330" height="292" rx="12" fill="#E0F2FE" opacity=".55"/>
  <text x="579" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#075985">the model's</text>
  <text class="t1" x="446" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#075985">a draft to argue with</text>
  <text class="t2" x="446" y="192" font-size="13" fill="#075985">the figure, drawn to the rules</text>
